# Clutter

Clutter is each mark on a picture of data that is not data and does not help to read them: a grid, a frame, a divider, a fill, a decoration. It is not neutral. Marks act on each other, and a strong structure is seen before the data that it holds. This file is about what to remove from a chart, a table or a block of numbers, and how to keep the few aids that help.

## The share of ink that carries data

Ink is each mark that is drawn, as opposed to the background. The measure of a picture of data is the share of its ink that carries data. Raise it: say the same with less ink.

- **Erase, and see if the meaning is lost.** One bar with its value "56" written above it says 56 in six ways: the height of its left edge, of its right edge, the place of its top, the height of its fill, the place of the number, and the number. Take away the base, the edges and the fill one by one: the meaning stays. What is left is the number, the one exact way.
- **A picture is only for a comparison.** With one number, a chart adds nothing: write the number. From two numbers on, a picture can help the eye to compare them. Keep each mark that helps to compare or to see a pattern, and remove the others.
- **Ink costs nothing on a screen, and still it costs**: each mark acts on the others (see below), thus more lines, colors and elements leave less of the data to see.
- **Less ink must not lose the nature of the data.** Bars for periods, thinned to lines, lose the width that says "a period". Reduced to dots at their tops, the dots are joined by the eye into a line that does not exist. A short level line across the width of each period keeps the value and the period with the least ink.
- **A mark that says a thing by its shape frees a color.** A candle of a price chart says rise or fall by black or white. A small tick to the left for the opening value and one to the right for the closing value say it by shape, and then the thick body can go.
- **A table has ink to save in its words too**: the same words in each cell go into the heading or the title, and a value that is not of the same type as the rows (the country in a table of regions) goes out of the table as a line below it. The saved space can take more data: blocks of the same structure need their column headings only one time.
- **A table in which each column has one value is one sentence**: "Seats 6 to 12 in row 4".

## Do not spend strong means on weak things

Each means of emphasis loses its force when you use many: this is the inflation of means.

- **The common thing gets the lightest mark.** If each plain stop of a network map is a full circle, a stop where lines cross needs a frame around its circles to differ, and a crossing of three lines is a heavy knot. With a small tick for a plain stop, a plain circle is enough for a crossing.
- **Do not give a mark of its own to a difference that the reader does not care about** (a line of a different technical type). That mark then needs its own variant for each state (planned, closed), the variants need their own marks for crossings, and the least important object of the picture gets the loudest sign.
- **A weak state looks weak**: a thing that is planned or not active is paler and thinner than the real ones, not a dashed line that vibrates and draws the eye more than a solid one.
- **Leave room.** A picture that has used all its means cannot take one more type of information.

## A new form for people who work with the old one

A cleaner form is not put in the place of a form that people read by habit in work where seconds or lives count (a trader, a surgeon, a dispatcher). There, offer the new form next to the old one for a long time, and tell the user that the change is a risk of its own.

## Marks make marks that you did not draw

- **1 + 1 = 3 or more.** Two lines make a third thing, the band between them. Each mark also acts with the edges of its area and with its neighbors. Ten tiles on colored backgrounds make a white grid that nobody drew, and that grid is the strongest thing on the screen.
- **Contrast makes it stronger.** A grid of thick dark bars makes spots flicker at its crossings.
- **Regularity makes it stronger.** The eye finds a pattern that repeats before each content inside it. Equal dark and light stripes vibrate, and the person cannot count them.
- **A line that separates also joins.** Vertical bars between the items of a menu glue the items into one string; a gap separates them better. A frame with a shadow around each of two neighbors gives three lines between them.

## Remove the aid, then give back the least

- **Start with no grid, no frames and no fills.** Things that stand near each other and apart from the rest are seen as one thing with no line (the rule of distance in the skill `canvas-screen-design`). If a table cannot be read with no grid, its layout is wrong: repair the layout.
- **An aid is weaker than the data**, always: thinner and paler than the line of the chart, the digits of the table, the notes on the staff. If the line of a grid is as thick as the stroke of a digit, the grid wins.
- **A grid behind a chart** was for a person who drew the chart by hand. Now it only helps the reader to see through which values the line goes. Draw it thin and pale behind the data, or as small marks at the axis, or leave it out.
- **A structure that carries meaning stays, but second.** The lines of a music staff say which note it is, and the cells of a map index say where to look. Draw them light (thin, pale, dotted), thus the content is read first and the structure is found when it is needed.
- **Use fewer, lighter means for the same division.** To part the columns of a dense timetable, a pale background under the time column does more than a thick rule, with less ink. A rare strong break (one for each hour) does not form a regular grid.
- **Remove the background of a chart area and the dividers between bars.** A colored area behind bars makes a second set of shapes that hang from the top. Bars differ by their height; they need no outlines.
- **Join neighbors.** A count that sits on its button is cleaner than a count in its own frame next to the button. A block that reaches the edge of the screen leaves no frame of background around it.

## Data need no decoration

- **Do not decorate a table or a chart because the data look dull.** The reader cannot tell decoration from data: does a darker shade mean a higher degree of something? Each decoration is a false signal.
- **No picture behind a chart**, and no map behind a list of towns unless each town stands at its place on the map.
- **No pictograms for counts** (ten birds for ten thousand messages). Numbers say it themselves, and a row of equal pictures is a regular pattern.
- **A sheet of unrelated numbers with illustrations is not a display of information.** If the numbers have no common unit, source or question, the picture has no content. Write a clear text with the numbers that matter.
- **A process drawn as colored steps must have a process in it.** If the first step is the whole task and the second holds all that is hard, an arrow that points at the thing says the same with less.
- **Clutter can hide a thing on purpose**: a warning in a heavy frame, in narrow capital letters, underlined, is seen and not read. Do not set important text in this way: no capitals for running text, no tight frame, normal letter spacing.
- **The differences must stand out, not the sameness.** In a timetable where each row says "daily", the one row "on work days" is lost. Say the common value one time, and mark the exception.
- **Beauty is welcome next to the data, not in them.** A photo that belongs to the story stands at the side of the chart as an illustration. A clean table can be printed on fine paper.

## People ask for the lines back

When frames and grids go, people who knew the old look complain for about two weeks, and then nobody wants them back. If the user asks to remove clutter from a screen that exists, say that this reaction is usual and passes.

## What to draw

- A table with no grid: one thin line under the heading at most.
- A chart with no background and no outlines, and a grid that is paler than the data or absent.
- Structures that carry meaning in thin, pale lines.
- No decoration inside the area of the data.
